**Sūrat al-Raḥmān ʿAzza wa-Jalla** (The Sūrah of the Most Merciful, Mighty and Majestic)

It is also called *ʿArūs al-Qurʾān* (the Bride of the Qur'an).

Its purpose is to demonstrate what the Sūrat al-Qamar concluded with: the greatness of His dominion and the completeness of His power, through the all-encompassing nature of His mercy and the precedence of His mercy over His wrath. This is indicated by the completeness of His knowledge, from which the comprehensiveness of His power necessarily follows. That is indicated by the detailed display of the wondrous marvels of His creatures and the amazing products of His making, in a style of reminding of His bounties and bestowing favor through His abundant blessings. It is presented in a manner that produces knowledge of His encompassing all the attributes of perfection. Its primary purpose, therefore, is to establish the attribute of all-encompassing mercy, as an encouragement toward His beneficence and kindness and as a warning against His vengeance, by cutting off the increase of His favor. The name of the Sūrah, *al-Raḥmān*, indicates this, because He is the One whose favor is universal. Its name *ʿArūs al-Qurʾān* is also clear in this regard, because it contains what is in it of adornments and fine garments, jewels and crowns, and the bride is characterized by all blessings, beauty, radiance, and perfection of their kind.

(In the name of Allah), whose all-encompassing perfection is manifested through the marvels of His creation. (The Most Gracious), whose universal mercy is manifested through the dazzling wonders of His making and the renowned greatness of His signs and clear proofs. (The Most Merciful), whose special favor toward the people of His obedience is manifested through their realization, by adhering to His worship, of the humility that yields honor.

* *

When Glorified is He concluded the Sūrat al-Qamar with the greatness of dominion and eloquent power, and since a sovereign who has power does not perfect his dominion except through mercy, and since His mercy is not complete except through its universality, He restricted this Sūrah [p. 140] to enumerating His blessings upon His creation in both abodes. That is among the effects of dominion. He detailed in it what He had summarized at the end of al-Qamar regarding the abode of the friends and the enemies in the Hereafter. He began it with the name that indicates the universality of mercy, as an excellent opening for the beginning, and as a counterpart to what is obtained through dominion and power of ultimate blessing, manifestation, awe, and dread. He did this with a name that, despite being in utmost concealment, indicates the greatest hope. He opened it with the greatest of blessings, which is teaching the Remembrance (the Qur'an), which stirred those of lofty resolve in al-Qamar to turn toward it, with His saying: ﴿And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there anyone who will remember?﴾ [al-Qamar: 17]. This is because the "We" in "yassarnā" (We made easy), which indicates greatness and is the pillar of dominion, has two aspects: the aspect of majesty and omnipotence, which requires that He speak in a way that defeats His creation from every direction in understanding, memorization, producing its like, and every meaning within it; and the aspect of honor and mercy. Since His mercy preceded His wrath, He looked upon His creation with it, especially this merciful Ummah. So He made the Remembrance easy for it, realizing mercy after having left, from the traces of omnipotence, the inimitability (*iʿjāz*) that prevents looking. Among what prevents understanding from grasping it is the disjoined letters (*al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa*) at the beginnings of the sūrahs. He also prevented the perverse one from saying that they have no meanings, by enabling [some of] the chosen ones to understand some of their secrets. He said, answering one who seemed to ask: Who is this Sovereign, the Powerful? It was said: ﴿al-Raḥmān﴾, that is, the One whose mercy is universal. Ibn Burjān said: "It is the outward aspect of His name Allah and the inward aspect of His name al-Rabb. He placed these three names, in their manifestation, in the station of the Essence, reporting about Him through them and making them a veil between Him and His creation, through which He conveys address from Him to them. Then His other manifest names clarify these three names." End.

From the requirement of His name ﴿al-Raḥmān﴾ all blessings have spread forth, and for this reason He mentioned in this Sūrah the foundational blessings of both abodes.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 2:

Since nothing of mercy is more eloquent, and nothing is more indicative of power, than conveying some of the Creator's attributes to the created in a certain manner, so that they may take on those attributes to the extent they are able, and thereby attain eternal life and everlasting happiness, He said: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾. That is, the visible and witnessed [Qur'an] in writing, and the recited [heard] [Qur'an], which gathers all good and distinguishes between every confusion. Analogy would require that no one know the heard [Qur'an], since it is one of His attributes, and His attributes are as great as His essence, and His essence is pure unseen, because creation is too lowly to encompass Him in knowledge. "And where is the Pleiades from the hand of one who reaches for it?" So His teaching the Qur'an indicates that He is able to teach whatever He wills to whomever He wills: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. The appropriateness of placing this before all the other blessings is clear, because the most excellent of blessings is the blessing of religion (dīn), which is followed by the blessing of this world and the Hereafter. It is the highest rank. It is the summit (sanām) of the heavenly books, their pillar, their confirmation, and their interpreter (al-ʿabbār ʿalayhā). Its benefit is conveying [people] to the "seat of truthfulness" in the presence [of the King] (maqʿad al-ṣidq), since it clarifies what pleases God so that it may be acted upon, and what angers Him so that it may be avoided.

Imam Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: It is known that the Glorious Book, although all its verses are dazzling miracles and its surahs, in their sublime composition and wondrous arrangement, are decisive against adversaries and overpowering, some of them are clearer than others in showing their inimitability (iʿjāz) and in the manifestation of their eloquence and conciseness. Do you not see how minds rush to grasp the eloquence of certain verses and surahs at first glance, without much reflection, such as His, exalted is He: ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold"﴾ [Hud: 44], and His saying: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded and turn away from the polytheists﴾ [al-Hijr: 94], and the verses like them? None hesitates regarding their dazzling inimitability except one whom God has sealed upon his heart, or whose door of understanding He has blocked, so how could he enter or knock upon it? The surah of al-Qamar is of this kind. Do you not see the brevity of its stories, while its essential elements are present and its purposes fulfilled, and what accompanies each story of admonition, exhortation, warning and giving excuse? Had I not intended to limit myself to commentary, I would have clarified what I pointed to of the order of the surahs, which I have not been preceded in, and perhaps God, glorified is He, will facilitate that in the tafsir that is in hand, may God benefit by it and make it easy in it. When this surah encompassed what we have mentioned, and the great mercy appeared in it through the repetition of stories and the pairing of admonitions, and God's proof upon creation became manifest, and this was among the greatest of His subtle kindnesses toward whoever He facilitates for him the contemplation of the Qur'an and grants him success in understanding it and reflecting upon it, He followed that, glorified is He, with calling attention to this blessing, and so He said, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ [al-Rahman: 1], ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, ﴿He created man﴾ [al-Rahman: 3], ﴿He taught him the expression﴾ [al-Rahman: 4]. He singled out this name from His most beautiful names, as an indication of His mercy through the Book and His great benevolence in it: ﴿And if you tried to count God's blessings, you could not enumerate them﴾ [al-Nahl: 18]. Then it has been established that the surah of al-Qamar is a giving of excuse. And from where would the servants have, through this beautiful kindness and this great forbearance, that they should be returned to the extension of proofs and the clarification of evidence, if it is difficult for them to have further explanation? So He, exalted is He, informed that this is mercy, and said: ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ [al-Rahman: 1], ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾. Then, if you reflect upon the surah of al-Qamar, you will find its address and its giving of excuse specific to the children of Adam, indeed only to the polytheists of the Arabs among them. So the surah of al-Rahman was placed after the surah of al-Qamar, as an alert to both species (al-thaqalayn) and an excuse given to them, and as an affirmation to both kinds (al-jinsayn) of what He, glorified is He, deposited in the world of wonders and manifest proofs. Thus the affirmation and the alert are repeated in it through His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So which of the blessings of your Lord will you deny?﴾ [al-Rahman: 13], addressing both kinds and giving excuse to both species. Thus its connection to the surah of al-Qamar became clearest of all clarity. (End.)

Since it is as if it were said: "How did He teach him?" — and this is one of His attributes, and "to whom did He teach him?" — He said, beginning anew or giving a reason: ﴿He created man﴾, that is, He decreed him and brought him into existence in this known form and described composition, separated from all inanimate things, though his origin is from them, then from all growing things, then from other animals. He made him into kinds, distinguished each people by their language from those other than them. His creating him is a proof of His creating every existing thing: ﴿Indeed, We created everything according to a measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49]. Although al-Insan (man) is a generic noun, the one most deserving of being meant by this is its first instance, who is Adam, peace be upon him. And his being meant, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said, does not prevent the generic meaning from being intended as such.

Since it is as though it were said: "Then what of His creating man?", He said: ﴿He taught him the bayan (clear expression)﴾, which is the speaking faculty. It is the perception of universal and particular matters, and of the present and the absent, by inferring the absent from the present, sometimes through tawassum (discerning character from outward signs), sometimes through hisab (calculation), at times through 'iyafa (divining by the flight of birds) and zajr (augury), and at other times through contemplation of the horizons and other things; along with discrimination between the good and the bad, and other matters that He, glorified and exalted, has deposited in him. It also includes his expressing what he has perceived by means of what is hidden in his inner self, and conveying it to others sometimes by speech and sometimes by action, whether by utterance, writing, gesture, or otherwise. Thereby he became capable of perfecting himself and of perfecting others. This is the teaching of bayan that enabled him to be taught the Qur'an. Although He, glorified be He, has instilled this in us and created us with it, and it has become familiar, well known and recognized among us, it is among others otherwise, in addition to what He, glorified be He, has made clear to us as a blessing upon us, by His disputation with His noble angels concerning our father Adam, peace be upon him, and by what He displayed to them of His knowledge, and by what He dazzled them with regarding the designation of every thing by its meaning and its name.

Since the Exalted had explained the blessing of teaching the Qur'an, which is the life of souls, and had explained the way to it, He pointed to clarity (al-bayan) by mentioning the clear signs that one command brings together and another separates, and which have a role in the life of bodies. He enumerated them as a favour, making them clear, because they are among the greatest blessings. So, in answer to one who asked, "What is its clarity?", He began with the greatest luminary, which is the greatest in light, the largest in body, and the most widely beneficial, so that its submission to the reception of effects would be a stronger proof of the submission of others. This is to show His wisdom in governing and His power in determining: ﴿The sun﴾, which is the sign of the day, ﴿and the moon﴾, which is the sign of the night, by which the Ibrahimi clarity (al-bayan al-Ibrahimi) occurred. Perhaps He began with the end of their clarity for this community, honouring it by pointing to the height of its understanding, peace be upon him. ﴿By a reckoning﴾, that is, their motion: each of them moves, despite their sharing the fact that they are two heavenly luminaries, by a reckoning so precise that its majesty can hardly be described in its exactness, its vast extent, and the greatness of the religious and worldly benefits that branch from it. From the greatness of this reckoning, which the form al-Fu'lan conveys, is that it follows a single course which it does not exceed. By it the years, months, days, hours, minutes and seasons are known, in fixed stations, and the position of each of them in the upper horizons is known, along with what happens to it and what is affected by it in the lower world, such that by it most lower affairs are regulated, and so on with the other matters for which God created them and for which they were created. Between a human being and each of them lie distances that none knows precisely except the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. This, over the lengthening of days and ages, does not disturb even an atom, a proof that its Maker is the Self-Subsisting who never heeds not. Then, after this renewed reckoning comes the greater reckoning, which He determined for the folding up of the sun and the eclipsing of the moon, a proof that He acts by choice, together with what this implies of the succession of the two alternations: at times in balance, at times in increase, and at others in decrease, and other matters among the subtleties of what is decreed.

(p-146) Since their course along this path, with the constant toil it demands of them in change and movement, is an act of obedience on their part to the One who arranges them, originates them, and sets them in motion, and since their submission, though they are the two greatest luminaries, points by a fortiori reasoning to the submission of what is beneath them of the stars, their mention made unnecessary the specific mention of everything else. So He followed them with mention of what stands to the earth as the stars stand to the sky in adornment, benefit, harm, smallness, greatness, abundance, and scarcity, namely the plants. He put the small ones first, because of the generality of their benefit and the great effect they have, since most foodstuffs for all animals come from them, as do clothing materials such as cotton and flax, and other wondrous matters. He expressed this in terms that suit the rest of the stars, saying: ﴿And the star﴾, that is, all the heavenly stars, and every plant that rises from the earth and has no stem, from the earthly plants, which are the basis of the sustenance of humans and all other animals. ﴿And the tree﴾, that is, everything that has a trunk and is used for fruit or for food. ﴿Prostrate themselves﴾, that is, they submit and comply with what is intended by them, and they are humbled to be useful, in the manner of a prostrating rational being obeying what he is commanded, by their movement as they were subjected to that purpose and by their obedience to what they were ordained to be, without refusal, through the renewal of times: growth in the plants, standing, greening, drying, bearing fruit, and withering. The star cannot rise to the rank of the tree, nor can the tree descend to the depth of the star; and so on with other matters, among which We have turned the prostration of shadows and the movement of mountains (p-147) and the example, which indicate the oneness of the Maker and that He acts by choice, and the negation of natures; and among them the direction of the stars and the arrangement of benefits in heat and cold, by which He, glorified is He, established the balance in plants, in fruits and foodstuffs, and other aspects of benefit.

When the change of what came before, namely the sun, the moon, the star, and the tree, clearly shows that He, glory be to Him, is the one who affects them, and since the heaven and the earth remain fixed in one unchanging state, their matter could have been obscure, just as a group of people went astray about them. Among them were the people of wahda (the doctrine of the oneness of existence), the people of stagnation and deception, those who stop at the witnessed world, and others. When it is established that He, exalted is He, is the one who affects them, He said, attributing the effect to Himself, after stripping what precedes them of any like of it, because the indication by change, motion, and transition had already sufficed. This is coordinated with an implied meaning: "And He is the One who arranged all that." ﴿And the heaven, He raised it﴾, meaning, sensibly, after it had been joined to the earth. He parted it from the earth and lifted it above it, and reason testifies to this for everyone who reflects, since every heavy body is not lifted above what lies beneath it except by a lifter, and there is no lifter for this heaven except God, for no one other than Him is able to exert such an effect. Because of its greatness, He placed it before the verb, drawing attention to reflection on what it contains of the majesty of His craftsmanship and the varieties of His wonders. The meaning also includes that He made it the place where His decrees originate, the source of His judgments, the descent point of His commands and prohibitions, and the abode of His angels who descend with revelation to His prophets.

When the heaven, despite its loftiness, which indicates the might of its Originator and Arranger, (p-148) also indicates His justice through the balance of all its conditions, namely heat, cold, rain, snow, dew, drizzle, and other things, in that every season is balanced against its opposite, and He does not send it down except in a known measure, otherwise the earth would be entirely corrupted, it also points to the fact that He has legislated for us a similar justice, so that our conditions may be sound and our words and deeds may be upright, by that through which the heavens and the earth are sustained. So He said: ﴿And He set up the balance﴾, meaning the justice by which the two horizons (east and west) were made to rest, which is balance, that is, equilibrium, so that our affairs may be put in order.

When He first mentioned the Qur'an, which is the balance (mizan) of known things, and indicated its Merciful nature through various kinds of clear exposition, by which the human being is elevated until he becomes fit for understanding, and reminded him of the blessing of the balance for perceptible things, He turned to address him directly, diverting him from the third-person style. This was to energize him toward ascending the ranks of perfection through good compliance, and He gave the reason, saying: "that" (an), i.e., [because] "do not transgress" (la taṭghaw), i.e., do not exceed the limits ﴿in the balance﴾, meaning in the things that are weighed, among known weighable things, and in knowledge and action, each measured against the other, and in the equality of the outward and the inward, and of speech and deed. Thus the second "balance" is general, covering both the balance of known things and the balance of perceptible things.

Since the intended meaning was: "Follow My actions and take on the character of everything I command you in My words," He followed this with His saying: ﴿And establish the balance﴾, that is, all the actions by which things are measured ﴿with justice﴾.

Since the intended meaning is great justice, He clarified it by emphasis after the command, following the command with a prohibition against the opposite (p-149), so He said: ﴿And do not make deficient the balance﴾, that is, do not cause any deficiency in an instrument of justice by which things are measured—such as the measuring rod, the scale, the balance and the measure, or the like—which is a kind of loss, by what is indicated by the bare form of the verb, "so that you would lose the balance of your deeds and your recompense on the Day of Resurrection." It is known from the repetition of "the balance" what emphasis is intended in the command concerning it, because of its great importance, whether it is with one meaning or with different meanings.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 10:

When He mentioned His favour, which indicates His power by raising the sky, He mentioned its counterpart in the same manner, after placing between the two what they both upheld of justice, as an alert to the intensity of care and concern for it. So He said: ﴿And the earth﴾, that is: and He placed the earth. Then He explained the one who set it (its establisher) so that it would be like what was mentioned twice, as an indication of the greatness of His arrangement because of the intensity of the wisdoms within it. So He said: ﴿He set it﴾, that is: He spread it out and extended it over the water, ﴿for the creatures﴾, that is, for every being that has the capacity to sleep or the capacity for the *wanīm*, which is the sound (the cry or noise of living creatures), after He had set up for them the balance (*mīzān*) on which the earth does not stand except by it.

[p. 150]

Since the passage was explaining mercy through abundant favours, and establishing the proof was the greatest blessing, and fruits are the most delightful of things, and their delicacy and extreme fineness made them incompatible with the earth in its dryness and density, their existence in it was a wonder indicating His great power. Mentioning them also points to the blessings that precede them, all the staple foods. So he began with them, so that what precedes them would be like what is mentioned twice. He then said, resuming, describing them in a more general way: ﴿In it is fruit﴾, meaning kinds of it, very great, which a person perceives, by his faculty of expression (bayan, clear discernment), to differ in forms, colours, tastes and benefits, and other wondrous matters.

Since the purpose of indefinite form (tankir) in describing it was to magnify it, he drew attention to this by specifying one of its kinds, and singled it out because it combines enjoyment with sustenance. It is the most prominent of the fruits of the Arabs, who are the primary intended audience of this mention. So he said: ﴿And the palm﴾. He indicated complete power by his saying: ﴿having sheaths﴾, meaning possessing the coverings (akmam, sing. kimam) of its fruit, which is the spathe (ṭalʿ) before it splits open with the fruit. Every plant that produces something enclosed in a covering has a kimam, but the term is especially well known for the palm because of its nobility and fame among them. Al-Baghawi said: "Every thing that covers something is a kimm and a kummah, and from it comes the kumm of a shirt (sleeve)." In this there is a reminder of the fruit of Paradise that splits open to reveal what is within. He mentioned the palm tree itself rather than only its fruit, to draw attention to the abundance of its benefits, from its fibre, its palm fronds, its palm leaves, its trunks and other benefits, beyond the fruit.

When he mentioned what is eaten as food from fruits, which is of great length, he followed it with the root of sustenance for people and livestock, which is quite brief. He said, mentioning its fruit because it is the thing intended in itself: ﴿And the grain﴾, i.e., of wheat and other grains. He drew attention to the completeness of power, after an earlier reminder through the distinction of these items, although the origin of all of them is water, by his saying: ﴿and the husk﴾, i.e., the leaves and herbage, which, when the weight of the grain is removed from it, becomes what the winds sweep away and scatter. This is the chaff, which is part of the fodder of livestock.

Since al-rayḥān (sweet basil) is applied specifically to every plant of fragrant scent [and in general to every plant], he followed it with it so that it covers and singles out all that was mentioned of the other plants and beyond. This is a way of reminding of His blessings through nourishment of the spirits, after having mentioned nourishment of the bodies. So he said: ﴿and the sweet basil﴾.

Since the Lord, glory be to Him, is disbelieved in by one who denies Him or denies some of His attributes, or who denies one of His messengers, that person has denied His blessings or one of them. By denying that one blessing, he is bound to deny all blessings, because the messengers call people to God by reminding them of His blessings. The portion of this surah up to this point consists of twelve verses, according to the counting of the Kufan and Syrian (verse-count) traditions. In these verses He enumerated the principal blessings bestowed by Him, glory be to Him, in a manner that by the utmost clarity indicates that He possesses every perfection. This number is the first increasing number, signifying the multiplication of blessings, because its fractions, namely the half, third, quarter and sixth, exceed its base. The two species, jinn and humankind, were mentioned earlier in His words, "al-anam" (the creatures). God, exalted is He, said this to indicate that they are the intended audience of the admonition, rebuking, reproaching and silencing whoever denies any of His blessings, or says a statement, or does an act, that necessarily entails denying some of them. This follows from the enumeration of these increasing blessings, which cannot rightly be denied, nor can any part of them be denied, so gratitude for them is obligatory. So: ﴿So which of the favours﴾, that is, the bounties and gifts, ﴿of your Lord﴾, that is, the One who has done good to you by the favours He has bestowed upon you, in a manner of majesty and greatness, and these favours are lasting and do not cease, without any need to reciprocate from anyone or anything else, ﴿O you two hosts (of creation)﴾, the One who governs you, besides whom there is no governor or master for you, from His signs, His crafts, His wisdom and His might in His creation, and the submission of all to Him and the subjugation of you two to Him. Indeed, all these great blessings are signs indicating Him, firm crafts, judgments and wisdoms through which His might appears and His power becomes manifest. ﴿Will you deny?﴾ So His addressing the two hosts with this shows that these things encompass the jinn just as they encompass humankind, and that they have a share in them just as humankind does. Mentioning this verse after this number of signs indicates that the blessings increase to a degree that cannot be counted, such that their enumeration is beyond the grasp of the minds of the responsible beings, lest they suppose that there is no blessing other than what is mentioned in this surah. Its expression by the word ālā' (favours) is because these are the blessings specific to kings, on account of their radiance and the distinguishing row (of splendour) that sets them apart from others, and because of the good and the supplication involved in seeing them. Although it may derive from the root ʾ-l-w (to be lofty or to delay), it is possible to take it from lu'wā' (a hardship), the original root being hamza and lām. When another lām or an alif is added to them, the meaning that was apparent increases, because the alif conceals the hamza and its inner aspect, and the lām is the very essence of what was there, so no departure from that meaning occurs. If you consider āl (the family/return), the meaning is that these great royal blessings make manifest to the servants the knowledge of Him, glory be to Him, and that everything ultimately returns to Him without dispute, just as He was the possessor of everything. The piercing eyes grow weary of looking at them, just as they grow weary of seeing the figures that the mirage raises, because they point to Him, glory be to Him... (p. 153) they are great blessings, even if they are also punishments, for there is no blessing that indicates Him in the way that He does. He repeated this verse in this surah from here after every verse to its end, because of what preceded regarding the moon: when a denier repeatedly denies something with great insistence, to the point of burning hearts in open obstinacy, it is fitting to enumerate what he denied, and each time one is reminded of a single instance of it, it is said to him: why do you deny it? Whether he acknowledges it at the moment of confirmation or persists in obstinacy, the repetition here serves to make clear that his denial has exceeded all bounds. And because the blessings differ, are multiple and varied, it is good to repeat the reproach concerning them one by one, to draw attention to their greatness. If it is a blessing, the matter concerning it is clear; if it is a punishment, then the blessing lies in averting it or delaying its onset. Since it was earlier stated that every reminder of what God, exalted is He, has bestowed of blessings through the five senses, which operate in the six directions, you will find, if you consider the verse itself, that it points to this. Each of its words, except the last in the spelling of those who wrote the alif in the rasm (the consonantal orthography of the codices), consists of five letters if you count the spelling of the first two and the third as five in the rasm, six in the hijā' (orthographic spelling) and in pronunciation. So they correspond to the senses and the directions, because all is from the Lord. The last word consists of six letters if you consider its rasm in the mushafs (codices) that omitted its alif, for there is disagreement among the imams of the mushafs regarding its inclusion and omission. It indicates the directions, because these are what a person has the power to dispose of, whereas the senses are not within his choice. If you consider its spelling according to pronunciation, it is seven letters, indicating that the blessings (p. 154) are more than can be counted, due to what preceded regarding the secrets of the number seven, and indicating that the denial of the responsible beings is very widespread. Therefore it is most appropriate that these blessings be spread out according to the number of the five senses multiplied by the six directions, and in reality this is a benefit. For it is well known and commonly recognized, and an admirable quality described, that repetition in the face of denial necessitates repetition in the face of confirmation, and brings it to the utmost in beauty of effect. The number exceeded the flat product of five times six by one, indicating that the blessings of the one (God) have no cessation. Therefore it was subdivided into eight, which were mentioned first after the blessings, so it was in the number of seven, which is the first perfect number, for it combines the odd and the even, the even of the odd, and the even of the even. It exceeded it by one to indicate that whenever a cycle of a perfect number is completed, it is worthy of other blessings, and these are unending, because the One who bestows them possesses complete power and perfect knowledge, and His mercy precedes His wrath. In their being eight there is an indication that they are a means to the Garden with eight gates, if they are thanked for. In following them with seven fiery ones there is an indication that they are a cause for the Fire with seven gates, if they are disbelieved. In following them with these there is an indication that their causing of the Fire is closer, because they are surrounded by desires. In this is an indication that whoever guards against what he is threatened with, by thanking for these blessings, is protected from the seven gates of the Fire. Then He followed them with eight, in which He mentioned the Garden of those brought near, indicating that whoever acts for what he has been promised, as God commanded him, attains the eight gates of the Garden. And eight others following the Garden of the companions of the right, indicating the same, and God knows best. Its arrangement was most excellent: the blessings were mentioned first, to win hearts and encourage thanks; then the terrors, as warning and as a means of averting corruption through disobedience and disbelief; then the lasting blessings, to draw in benefits. He began (p. 155) with the most noble of them, mentioning the Highest Garden, because the heart after being frightened is more alert, aspirations are higher, and resolve is stronger. Thus this first verse of the thirty-first (group) indicates that the blessing of sight is from the direction of the front, as if it were said: Will you deny the blessing of sight, which confronts you, or some other?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 14:

Since the blessing of the creation of man had already been mentioned in the indication of the address, and then He mentioned the roots of the blessings upon him in a wondrous manner, until He mentioned the nourishment of his spirit, the basil (al-rayhan), He followed that with a detailed explanation of what had been stated in summary, saying: ﴿He created man﴾, meaning the origin of this species, which is among the total of creatures (al-anam) for whom We created the basil, and the predominant trait in it is intimacy (al-uns) with itself and with what it has become accustomed to.

Since most of its elements is earth (al-turab), although it is one of the four elements, he expressed, as an indication of the correspondence of its name (insan, from nisyan/uns) with what it contains that requires intimacy, the result of which is steadiness in one state, for its named referent (musamma), most of which is earth, because of its heaviness and its stability unless a mover moves it. He expressed this by what is at the furthest extreme from the capacity for clear description, saying: ﴿from clay (salsal)﴾, meaning: dry earth that has a sound when it is struck upon, ﴿like pottery (al-fakhkhar)﴾, meaning: like fired earthenware baked with fire, because He took it from the earth, then mixed it with water until it became clay, then left it until it became black mud, moulded (masnun), altered (mubin). Then He shaped it as a jug and other vessels are shaped, then He dried it until it reached the utmost hardness, so it became like pottery which, when struck, makes a sound by which it is known whether there is a defect in it or not, just as the human being, by his speech, reveals his condition, the furthest end of his matter and his outcome. So what is mentioned here is the ultimate end of his creation, and this is more fitting to the Most Merciful (al-Rahmaniyya); elsewhere sometimes its beginning is mentioned and sometimes its formation. The earth is his mother and the water is his father, mixed with the air which carries the part that is of the blaze of Hell. So from the earth is his body and his self (nafs), from the water his spirit and his intellect, from the fire his error and his fierceness, and from the air his movement and his fluctuation between praiseworthy and blameworthy traits.

When the jinn, who are also included in the term *al-anam* (mankind and creatures), were created from the four elements, with fire predominating in their nature, God said: ﴿And He created the jinn﴾, meaning this species that is hidden from the eyes, created from their father. It is an *ism jam'* (collective noun) for *al-jinn*. Since *al-jinn* is also applied to the angels because they are hidden, he clarified that they are not meant here, saying: ﴿of smokeless fire﴾, meaning a pure, unmixed thing, extremely agitated and mixed. Al-Baghawi said: it is the clear part of the flame of fire that has no smoke in it. Al-Qushayri said: it is the flame mixed with the blackness of fire, end of quotation. Their fire was *maraja*, that is, mixed, with the cold of *al-Zamharir* (extreme cold). Since *al-marij* applies generally to fire and other things, he specified it by saying: ﴿of fire﴾, which is the predominant of its elements. Thus the intended meaning was fixed by mentioning fire, because the angels, upon them be peace, are of light, not of fire, and there is no agitation or turbulence among them; rather they are in the utmost steadfastness in obedience to what they were commanded. By this, every agitated being has been made aware of its measure, so that it does not transgress its limit. (p-157)

Since the creation of these two kinds upon these two aspects, which are in the utmost opposition, one of them hidden from the other, while each is prevented from dominating the other except rarely, as a manifestation of His great power and dazzling wisdom, which are among the greatest blessings, He said, consequently upon it: ﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ That is: the royal blessings arising from your Originator, your Nurturer and your Master. ﴿Will you deny?﴾ That is: the blessing of sight from behind and otherwise, of your creation upon this strange pattern, of His depositing in you what He deposited of faculties, of making you the essence of His creatures, and of preventing one of your two kinds from the other, and facilitating for you sustenance and benefits, and guiding you to the easy true religion (al-hanifiyyah al-samhah), and His power to restore you as He was able to originate you.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 17:

When He, glorified is He, had mentioned these two kinds, one of which is apparent and the other hidden, as guidance to reflect on what they contain of evidence for the perfection of His power, and since they both need the place they occupy, and since their well-being is among the things He, glorified is He, arranged, namely the stations of sunrise, which is the cause of light and manifestation, and sunset, which is the source of darkness and concealment, He followed it with His saying, alerting to contemplation of the wondrous workmanship that indicates His oneness: ﴿Lord﴾, that is, He is the Creator and Manager of ﴿the two easts﴾ and their Arranger, in a manner in which none other than Him has power over any part of it. ﴿And Lord of the two wests﴾ likewise. These easts and wests are: for winter, the constellations (burūj, zodiacal mansions) of the lower southern direction, which are the cause of rains and snows, which are the cause of life and manifestation, while the sun is descending in the horizons of the sky; and for summer, the high constellations in the northern direction, which are the cause of crushing and setting, while the sun is ascending in the atmosphere of the sky; and between them the spring, which is for growth, and the autumn, which is for withering. So they are a sign of bringing into existence and of annihilation.

The first of the easts is summer, at the time of equality of night and day, [when] the sun arrives at the first of the northern constellations while ascending, which is al-Kabsh (Aries). At that time the season becomes equal, through its southern parts and its receiving of the northern ones. Then the last of its easts is when the sun is at the end of the northern constellations and the beginning of the southern ones, at its arrival at ra's al-Mizan (the head of Libra). The season becomes equal a second time, for its receiving of the southern constellations. Then, by its arrival at the end of al-Qaws (Sagittarius) and ra's al-Jadi (the head of Capricorn), there is the conclusion in the shortness of days and the length of nights, due to its being in the middle of the southern constellations. Then, by its arrival in the same manner at its exit from the constellation of al-Tawamayn (Gemini) to al-Sarataan (Cancer), of the northern constellations, which is the last of the sun's degrees, there is the length of days and the shortness of nights. Thus heat and cold differ between these two seasons. The sun's being at the beginning of the constellation of al-Hamal (Aries) is equivalent to its rising from the east at the beginning of every day. Its being at the second equinox, when it receives the southern constellations upon arriving at ra's al-Mizan, is equivalent to its setting. Then its being at the two extremes in the length of days, at its arrival at the constellation of Cancer, is equivalent to its standing in summer at the midst of the sky, just as its arrival at ra's al-Jadi at the conclusion in winter, [in] the shortness of days and the length of nights, is equivalent to its standing, in what corresponds to its standing in winter, at the midst of the sky during the day.

This is what Ibn Burjan mentioned, and after that he said: He, glorified is He, subjected to His servants Jahannam, that is, by means of the sun, and it is the greatest enemy to them. Through it He brought forth for them both the crops, the olives, the pomegranates, the palm trees, the grapes, the gardens, the trellised and untrellised, and of all the fruits.

Since there are countless blessings in this, He said, giving the reason: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ — the One who arranged for you this great arrangement — ﴿deny﴾; that is, the blessing of sight, whether from the right side or otherwise, and the subjugation of the sun and the moon, both moving constantly and revolving, for regulating time, renewing the days, counting the months and years, the moderation of the air, and the variation of conditions in the manner suited to the interests of this world and its livelihoods, according to a preserved method and a law that does not deviate.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 19:

Since the open expanse of the sea, for the sailing of ships, is like the open expanse of the sky, for the movement of the stars, together with [what] the mention of the risings and settings necessitated, namely the inclusion, in the mention of the risings and settings, of the winter's rains, which occur in it to such a degree that, had they proceeded according to measure, they would have overflowed the seas, so that they would have drowned the deserts and wastelands, risen above the cities and all the regions, He said: ﴿He released﴾, i.e., sent forth, the Most Merciful, ﴿the two seas﴾, i.e., the salt and the sweet, making them agitated, agitation being part of their nature, while ﴿they meet﴾, i.e., they touch one another on the surface of the earth without any separation between them, in visible sight and in their inner depths. He made the sweet one a sign pointing to the waters of Paradise, and the salt one a sign pointing to a kind of drink of the people of the Fire, which does not quench the one who drinks it nor satisfy him, but burns his belly and wearies him. Or [the two seas are] the Persian Gulf and the Roman [Mediterranean] Sea, which "meet" in the Ocean because they are two inlets of it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 20:

When the meeting of the two fluids occurs, especially with constant turbulence and mixing, which transforms the attributes of one or both of them into the attributes of the other, the soul becomes eager to know what prevents such a thing between the two seas. He said, resuming: ﴿Between them is a barrier﴾, that is, a great barrier of pure power (in the first case) and of the disposition of the earth (in the second), which keeps them from mixing despite their meeting.

Ibn Burjan said: "The barrier (barzakh) is that which is neither the pure form of this nor the pure form of that. Likewise, the plain and the mountain have between them a barrier called al-khayf (the slope). Likewise, night and day have between them a barrier called ghabash (the dim twilight). Likewise, between this world and the Hereafter there is a barrier that is neither of this nor of that, nor is it outside of both. Likewise, the two springs are two barriers between winter and summer, like the dim light at the beginning of the day and the dim light at its end. He placed between every two kinds of existing things a barrier that is neither of this nor of that, and it is part of both, like the inanimate, the plant and the animal."

When the outcome of that was thus, He said: ﴿They do not transgress﴾, that is, they do not overstep in destroying people as they overstepped and destroyed those on the earth in the days of Nuh, peace be upon him (p-161), and neither of them oppresses the other by encroachment, nor do they exceed what their Creator and Governor has set as their limit, neither outwardly nor inwardly. Whenever you dig beside the salt water, you find sweet water, and the nearer you dig to it, indeed the sweeter it becomes. So God, glory be to Him, mixed them in the visible sense and separated them in the sense of the eye of power. And these are two inanimate things with no speech and no perception, so how can some of you transgress against others, O you who perceive and are rational?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 21:

Since this was a striking matter, clearly indicating the perfection of His power, especially with regard to the Hereafter, He said, deriving a consequence from it: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾, that is, the One who brought you into existence and nurtures you, ﴿will you deny?﴾, that is, the blessing of sight from the direction of the left or otherwise. Why did you not take heed from these foundational things among the kinds of existing beings, so that you would affirm the Hereafter, since you know through these intermediate states (barazikh) that this death of yours is an intermediate state (barzakh) and a separation between this world and the Hereafter, like the twilight (al-'isha') between night and day? And if you had sought to extrapolate this from the signs of the heavens and the earth, you would have found it prevalent in all the realms of existence.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 22:

When he had mentioned the favor of the sea, he mentioned the blessing by means of what grows in it, as he did with the land. So he said, expressing it in the passive voice, because each of its existence within it and the empowering over its extraction from it is an extraordinary matter without regard to a specific place of exit, and the blessing is the very act of coming out. For this reason, [Ghayr] Nafi' and the Basrans read with the active voice from the verb "to come out": ﴿yakhruju minhuma﴾ ("there come forth from both of them"), meaning: by the sweet water mixing with the salt water without an intermediary, or by means of the clouds. Thus that becomes like the male and the female. Al-Razi said: "So the sweet water is like the stallion to the salt water (i.e., the fertilizing agent)." Abu Hayyan said: The majority said: "It only comes forth from the salty water in the places where the rivers and sweet waters fall, so it is fitting that this be attributed to both of them, and this is well known among the divers." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and 'Ikrimah, his freedman, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "These things are in the sea through the descent of rain, because the oyster [and others] open their mouths to the rain." End.

So the oysters are like wombs for the drops, and the water of the sea is like the nourishing body. The evidence that it is from rain water is what the Ustadh Hamzah al-Kirmani said: "It is well known that when the year is barren, the fish become lean, and the oysters and pearls become few." End. Then, there is no doubt that although they are two seas, one attribute unites them, namely that both are [water], so it is permissible to attribute the coming forth to both of them, just as the coming forth of a person is attributed to the whole land, though he came out from one house within it. Likewise, the messengers are attributed to jinn and humans, by combining them in a single address, when He says: ﴿Messengers from among you﴾ [al-A'raf: 35], and similarly ﴿and made the moon in them a light﴾ [Nuh: 16], and many like these. ﴿The pearls (al-lu'lu')﴾, which is the pearl that is in the utmost whiteness, brilliance and clarity. ﴿And the coral (al-marjan)﴾, meaning the red branches that are in the utmost redness. So glory be to Him who differentiated between them in color, benefits and existence. Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted this statement from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "This is the most commonly used meaning." End. A large group said: the lu'lu' is the large pearls and the marjan is their small ones.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 23:

When that was among the great blessings, he made consequent upon it his saying: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ That is: the Owner of you both, who is the Greatest King, [while you deny] along with these great handiworks: is it the blessing of sight from the direction of above or other than that, the creation of benefits in the seas and your being given power over them, and the bringing forth of the wondrous ornaments and others?

Since He, glorified be He, mentioned the one that emerges from the sea by rainwater, He mentioned the one that travels upon it by the wind. By placing the prepositional phrase first, He indicates that the one traveling in the ship has no disposition of its own. And if some disposition appears to belong to it, it is, due to its weakness, like having no disposition at all. So He said: ﴿And His﴾, meaning: not to anyone else. Therefore do not be deceived by the apparent causes and stop at them, attributing any of that to them, as the people of deception by the visible did, who are the most rigid of the people of the earth in their minds and the most contemptible in their status, and who spoke of incarnation and unity. ﴿The ships﴾, meaning: the large and small ships, both empty and laden.

Since the life of everything is its existence in the state of its perfection, and since ships are built from assembled wood that is joined until it takes a form that receives many benefits, and since they are nurtured by that assembling just as plants and animals are nurtured, and since they rise upon the sea, their sails are raised, and they come into being in the sea after having been concealed by mountains of waves, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The produced (al-munsha'at)﴾. It is from nasha'a, meaning: when a thing comes to life and grows. A cloud is said to have "arose" (nasha'at) when it rose. The root meaning of nashi' is whatever came into being at night and began. The meaning of the reading of Hamzah and Abu Bakr, with the shin pronounced with a kasra (al-munshi'at), is that the ships raise their sails because they hold themselves steady against sinking, and that they bring about movement. The meaning of the reading of the rest of the readers (the reading with a fatha on the shin, al-munsha'at) is that the Maker produced them, sent them forth, and raised their sails.

Although they are high above the water, they are immersed in it, and although by their own nature they have nothing but sinking and submerging, He said: ﴿in the sea﴾. And since they are seen from a distance like mountains on the surface of the water, He said: ﴿like banners (al-a'lam)﴾, meaning: like tall mountains.

(p-١٦٤)

When the benefits in the sea, obtained through earning a livelihood by fishing and other means, and through reaching distant lands for immense gains, were present, and their work on the sea involved sincerity that necessarily carries over to sincerity on land, since both are equal in relation to His originating them and His power to direct them as He wills, He consequently said: ﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ That is, the greatest blessing. Will you deny the blessing of sight from beneath you, or of other journeys through places of peril, or of rescue when the sea is turbulent and the wind is in a place of loss, or of guidance to this after the creation of the materials of ships, the teaching of their craft, their subjection, and the ark (al-falak) lo-wahman bi-mathabat jami' al-kawn ("lo-wahman" as it stands in the text), so that its servants are like the angels in maintaining the dominion and in improving its coherence by the permission of their Lord? Those who travel in it, for whom it was created, are the equivalent of the commanded and obligated ones who are prepared, for whose sake the heavens, the earth and what lies between them were created. It carries them across from their exile to their place of settlement, and from their absence to their presence and their witnessing. Its manager stands at its top, commanding them with His command, so they worship Him and listen to Him.

Then the consideration may be turned so that it becomes a sign of the believer's passage through the days of this world. The world is the sea, the ship is his body, the inner self of the servant is the one carried in it, the intellect is its governing master, the faculties are its attendants, the command and management of God encompass it, faith is its security, divine success (al-tawfiq) is its wind, remembrance (al-dhikr) is its sail, the Messenger is its driver with what he brought from his Lord, and good deeds set its condition right. Ibn Burjan mentioned this.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 26:

When the Exalted One had informed that He created the heavens and the earth, and what He scattered within them of benefits [of substances] and meanings, and He completed the earth in its two divisions, land and sea, comprising within that the four elements upon which He founded compounds, and since the most wondrous of the creatures' crafts is what is in the sea, and its rider is in the status of non-existence, He indicated that He alone is the One who is singular in all of that, by the destruction of creation. So He said, resuming, expressing by the nominal sentence which indicates permanence, and by "man" (مَن) to indicate explicitness, as a way of magnifying the annihilation of the rational being [upon the annihilation of the non-rational being] by way of priority: ﴿Everyone upon it is passing away﴾, that is, upon the earth in its two divisions and also the heaven, ﴿will perish﴾, that is, destroyed and nonexistent in actuality, after he and others of all that [other than Him] were brought into being. There is nothing for all of that from its own essence except non-existence, so it is perishing in this respect. Although it exists, its existence lies between two non-existences: the first being that it had not been, and the second that it will cease. Then, in the interval between these, it is subject to bringing into being and annihilation at every moment of its states, its accidents and its powers, and the causes of destruction surround it, sensibly and in meaning, while it does not see them, just as they surround those who are in the ship, from above them, from below them, and from all their directions.

(p-166) Since the face is the most noble of all existing things, and it is used to refer to the one to whom the face belongs, even though the face cannot be conceived as subsisting without its owner, the expression of that reality by it is greater and more indicative of perfection. It is established among the people of the Sharia that He, glory be to Him, "there is nothing like unto Him" (Qur'an 42:11), so no one should imagine any deficiency from this expression. He said: ﴿And there remains﴾, i.e., after the passing away of all, a continuous subsistence without any end, ﴿the Face of your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who nurtures you with the message and raises you through this revelation to knowledge without limit, and every deed done purely seeking His Face, glory be to Him and exalted. When He mentioned His distinction from created things, He described Him with complete encompassing of perfection, with transcendence and praise, and said, describing the Face because the intended meaning is the essence (dhat), which is the most noble of it, using it as an expression, and because it is more eloquent than "owner," and with what alerts to His transcendence above what a dull, rigid person bound to sensible things might imagine from mention of the Face, who measures the Unseen, which is free of need and to whose most holy presence no deficiency can approach, by the witnessed, which is entirely deficiency and need: ﴿Possessor of Majesty﴾, i.e., the greatness that cannot be attained, which is an attribute of His essence, requiring His exaltation above everything unfitting to Him, ﴿and Bounty﴾, i.e., general beneficence, which is an attribute of His action.

Since death itself contains blessings that cannot be denied, and since the death of some people is a blessing upon others, together with what the verse concludes with of describing Him as the Bestower of favours, He said: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you deny?﴾ That is: [the One who nurtures you in this manner, whose end is to non-existence until a specified term] ﴿will you deny?﴾ That is: O you two groups (al-thaqalan), mankind and the jinn, is it the blessing of hearing from the front or other than it, from the bringing into being of creation and then their annihilation, and the succession of some of them after others, and the inheritance of some of what is in the hands of others, and similar matters, whose manner no one comprehends except Allah, the Exalted?

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 29:

Since need is the clearest proof of non-existence, and self-sufficiency (al-ghina) the clearest proof of the continuance of existence, he said, as a proof of what precedes it: ﴿Everyone in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾, meaning in a manner of continual renewal and persistence, ﴿everyone in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning all of them, whether speaking or silent, by the tongue of circumstance or of speech [or both]. And since it was as if it were said: "What does He do at the time of asking?", and "the day" (al-yawm) is the smallest of the defined and perceptible periods, he used it to express the smallest span of time, just as he expressed the lightest of weighed things by the atom (al-dharra). So he answered that by saying: ﴿Every day﴾, meaning every moment of the moments, from the day of Saturday, upon which be the curse and wrath of God, for they said about Saturday what is contrary to His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ [Qaf: 38], and ﴿And the preserving of them does not tire Him, and He is the Most High, the Most Great﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. ﴿He is in a matter﴾, meaning: of bringing into being substances and renewing meanings, or annihilating that. Al-Qushayri said: "[in] the varieties of the categories of created things and what He causes to pass over them of the differences of attributes." End.

It is matters that He manifests, not matters that He initiates anew, His power being attached in accordance with His will to what knowledge had attached in eternity, that it will exist or be annihilated at its times. Thus every thing is obedient to Him, submissive before Him, prostrate before His greatness, witness to His power, indicating Him. ﴿And there is not a thing but it glorifies Him with His praise﴾ [al-Isra: 44]. And that expression, although it is among the greatest of blessings, is the clearest proof of (p-168) the attributes of perfection [belonging to Him] and the attributes of deficiency for the changing things, and that they are non-existent in themselves, and because they are blessings. He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 30:

﴿Then which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ That is: the One who nurtures you both by this great management, for everything that makes you both righteous. ﴿Will you both deny?﴾ Is it the blessing of hearing, from [the direction of] behind or otherwise, or His directing of you in that for which He created you, which He knows better than you do, concerning your livelihoods and all your changes of state? This verse, which affirms the blessings from its beginning until here, has been repeated eight times following the blessings, indicating, and God knows best, that the blessing of God, glorified and exalted be He, cannot be counted, because it exceeds the seven, which is the complete number. The one is the starting point of a new cycle of numbers, indicating that whenever one cycle is completed, another cycle begins. Another aspect: in the last one, explicit mention is made of ﴿whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Rahman: 29], while the seven before it are specific to the people of the earth, indicating that the principal blessings are seven, like the heavens and the earth, the wandering planets, and the like.

When the enumeration of the great blessings had been completed in a manner that is, as far as expression allows, at the utmost extent of clarity, and since the changes of all other created beings, namely plants, inanimate things, angels, the heavens [and the earth], and whatever they contain, apart from the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan, jinn and humankind), follow a single order with no variation in it, while the states of the two weighty ones, owing to the conflict between intellect and appetites, can hardly be regulated, indeed the condition of one of them changes in a single moment into many contrary forms, because of the deceit in them, their states of contention, their transgression, their pursuit of self-interest, their frivolity, and their (response to) command and prohibition (p-169), and most of them die by their own fire without having avenged their own blood, wisdom required, and it was inevitable, that there must be for them a day on which they would gather, and in which a decisive judgment would be made between them by the scale of justice. He singled them out for mention and said, bringing the threat at the end, since after blessing and clarification there is for the disobedient nothing but a severe warning, calling them to return to obedience to the King, the Judge: ﴿We shall attend to you, O you two burdens﴾. The shift in the reading of the majority to the first-person plural (with nun) is more threatening than the reading of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i (qira'a, recitation) with the third-person yā', in keeping with what preceded. ﴿We shall attend﴾ means: by a near promise that admits no failure, concerning all the matters that have been mentioned. ﴿For you﴾ means: We act in the manner of one who turns wholly to a matter, so that he has no concern other than it, by the completion of Our hosts of angels and others in what We have commanded them, of what Our word has preceded and Our wisdom has carried out, concerning the terms of life, the provisions, and other things, so that all of it is brought to an end; then for them at that time there will be no task except gathering you so that He may judge between you. ﴿O you two burdens﴾ (ayyuhā al-thaqalān) with justice. The thiql (burden) is that by which the one who bears it is sustained; so it is as if the two were named thus by way of likening them to that, indicating that they are the ones principally intended among the creatures. Al-Razi said in al-Lawami': they are described thus to magnify their station, as if whatever else there is has no weight in comparison with them, and that is the end of his words. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I am leaving among you the two weighty things: the Book of Allah and my family (ʿitrah)." Ja'far al-Sadiq said: they were named so because they are weighed down with sins.

(p-170) Since this is among the greatest of the blessings upon which the servants depend, by which the lands are set in order, and by which the heavens and the earth stand, [and since] mere warning brings about the restraint of the soul from its spreading into what harms and does not benefit, how much more so the warning of the Day of Judgment (yawm al-fasl, the Day of Decision), He said: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ That is: to the One who does good to you both with this [well-wrought] creation. ﴿Will you both deny?﴾ Is it the blessing of hearing from the right, or other things, such as the rewarding of the people of His obedience and the punishing of the people of His disobedience? Ibn Burjan named this address, in which there is no plural nun (nun al-jam'), "the address of qabd" (contraction), in which He informs about His existents and what is their Creator. He said: "That is information from Him about pure Oneness. What precedes it, from ﴿We will attend to you﴾ [al-Rahman: 31] and the like, and what contains the plural nun, is information about the description of His dominion and His hosts, and it is the address of basț (expansion)."

Since the threat of "leisure" (al-faragh) might give the impression that they are now beyond reach, or that He is unable to deal with them or some of their affairs, He clarified, through the address of seizing (al-qabd), which manifests pure oneness (al-wahdaniyya), that they are in the grasp, and that none of them has any act of their own. The proof is that they do not attain all that they intend of what is within their capacity. But He concealed this by means of the causes through which restriction (al-taqayyud) is realized, ascribing matters to their immediate agents. So He said, explaining the intended meaning of "the two weighty ones" (al-thaqalan):

﴿O assembly﴾, i.e., O group in which there is capability, companionship and mutual friendship, ﴿of jinn﴾. He mentioned them first because of their greater strength and their penetrating influence in the pores, and their power to hide and to take forms, by which it was thought that nothing could overcome them. ﴿And humankind﴾, i.e., the select and those who are companionable and sociable, whose affair is built on settled residence and gathering.

When the intended meaning of the dual by this naming became clear, He used the plural to indicate their multitude, and said: (p-171) ﴿If you are able﴾ [i.e.,] if there is found in you obedience of existence in ﴿to pass through﴾, i.e., to traverse with your bodies and proceed without any barrier preventing you, ﴿beyond the regions﴾, i.e., the sides, ﴿of the heavens and the earth﴾, those in which a passage is opened for ease of penetration, for something you desire of fleeing from God, from carrying out retribution upon you, or of disobedience toward Him in accepting His judgments and the course of His wills and decrees concerning you, such as death or other than that, ﴿then pass through﴾. This indicates that each of them encompasses the other, because passing through does not truly occur except with piercing.

Since their passing through, in itself, was possible, but He prevented them from it by not creating its strength in any of them, especially since He has prevented them from it on the Day of Resurrection by matters among which is the encirclement of the people of the seven heavens [around them] row after row, and the enclosure of the Fire having surrounded the disbelievers, with no outlet for anyone except over the Bridge, which none crosses except every lean one who is light, He indicated this with His saying, resuming: ﴿You will not pass through﴾, i.e., [from] any of that, ﴿except with authority﴾, except with a great empowerment from Him, glorified is He, through a commanding decree and far-reaching power; and how could you have power to do that? Al-Baghawi said: "And in a report: the creation will be encircled by the angels and with a tongue of fire, then they will be called: 'O assembly of jinn...' the verse," end of quote. This is a narration of what will happen of that on the Day of Resurrection, not that it is specific to them.

[p. 172] When this was their state of contemplation regarding what lies between them and the rest of the animals, through the sensory and immaterial faculties He had given them, and through the rational ascents (al-maṣāʿid al-ʿaqliyya, the paths of reason) and the transmitted proofs (al-maʿārid al-naqliyya, the revealed evidences) that He had set up for them, by which they can penetrate to the ultimate limit of created beings and pass through, by the knowledge that leads them to it, to the highest of created beings; then (when He had) directed their contemplation to what lies between the animals and the plants, then between these and the inanimate things, clearly showing that He, glorified and exalted is He, gives to whom He wills what He wills, so that if He willed He would strengthen them to penetrate these (regions), and if He strengthened them to do so it would be among the greatest of blessings; and that He, glorified is He, is capable of whatever He wills concerning them, so if He willed He would destroy them, but He defers them to their appointed terms, out of His forbearance and His pardon toward them, He thereby made the following statement a consequence of that: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ That is: O (you two), the One who does good to you and nurtures you, by means of which you know His power over everything He wills. ﴿Will you deny?﴾ Is it the blessing of hearing, from the direction of the left or from other than it, by making you equal in that you cannot oppose His will, whether you are gathered together or alone; or by (the threat of) your being joined to the Day of Gathering, when He had already gathered you before, at the time He began your creation; or to the Day that is witnessed, when He had already made you witness against yourselves and bound you by covenant; or by the rending of the heavens, when you have seen the cloud rent after it had been spread out; or by the requital, when you have seen the swift requital and witnessed what befell the past nations.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 55, verse 35:

When He had removed from them the ability to pass through [the heavens and earth], as mentioned, this was a reminder that all power had been taken from them, and that whatever power they have is only by His decree, as a favour from Him to them. Among them were those who had reached the utmost hardness of heart and stiffness of thought (p-١٧٣), so that they attributed their inability to do certain things to the fact that no custom had been established for it, rather than to Him, glory be to Him, being the one who prevents it. So a portion of His wrath overtook them, and He said: ﴿A flame of fire will be sent against you﴾, meaning, O deniers. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: when [you come out of the graves] by being driven to the place of gathering, ﴿shuwaz﴾, that is, a great blaze, spreading and confined, surrounding you from every side, with a fierce sound, like one of narrow temper and intense anger.

Since shuwaz is applied to a flame that has no smoke, to the smoke of fire and its heat, and to other things, He clarified it with His words: ﴿of fire and brass﴾, meaning smoke that is extremely dreadful, in which there are flying sparks and molten copper. Ibn Jarir said: the Arabs call smoke nuhas, with the nun vowelled either with a damma or a kasra, and the reciters agreed on the damma, and that is the end of his words. Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read it in the genitive, as a conjunction with ﴿fire﴾, while the rest read it in the nominative, as a conjunction with ﴿shuwaz﴾.

Since this was possible both by reason and by custom, and they knew that if they fell into such a thing they would have no escape from it in any way, He made His saying ﴿so you will not be able to defend yourselves﴾ a consequence of it. Ibn Burjan said: this is the fulfilment of the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "A neck will come out of the fire and say, 'I am appointed over every obstinate tyrant,' and it will snatch them from among the throng as a hawk snatches a grain of sesame. The smoke of Hell will envelop the criminals, but it will not harm the believers among them. The sign of the shuwaz (p-١٧٤) and the neck of fire is there the thunderbolts of what is here, and its lightnings, and the well-known fire."

Since this threat is a kindness toward them, it is itself a blessing upon them, and the pardon of dealing with them by sending it is for that reason, He made the following statement its consequence: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ That is, the One who nurtures you both by repelling afflictions and bringing benefits, ﴿will you two deny?﴾ Is it the blessing of hearing from above or other than it? Did there not exist for you, in what you witnessed in this world, of the proofs of that and its signs, what necessitates for you faith?

When this was of a kind whose generality is not customarily established, though it digresses into its occurrence concerning some matters in scattered places, like many individuals, he (Allah) made its time clear to them by His saying: ﴿So when﴾, that is: as a consequence of this sending forth, when ﴿the sky is split open﴾ from its terror and magnitude, so that it becomes gateways for the descent of the angels and others, and other of Allah's signs. ﴿Then it becomes﴾, because of the heat that afflicts it, ﴿red (warda)﴾, that is: reddish, glowing from the intensity of its blaze. Al-Baghawi said: like the color of the rose-colored horse, which is the white that inclines toward redness and yellowness.

﴿like oil (ad-dihan)﴾, that is: melted and clear, like the substance with which one anoints, or like red leather and a slippery place. The sign of this in the world is the twilight redness at sunrise and at sunset. The answer to "idha" (when) is omitted; its estimate is: "You will know that with certainty of witnessing," or "How great the terror will be then." It is also possible that the answer is something indicated by the following verses, such as: "So on that day no one will be asked about his sin." Omitting it is more majestic, so that the imagination may go in every direction regarding it.

(p-175) Since preserving the sky from such things, by delaying the sending down of this [meteor] and others of the causes, and making them a place of the spirit, life and provision, is among the greatest of bounties, He said, as a consequence of it: ﴿So which of the bounties of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ That is: the One who nurtures you both in this perfectly-wrought arrangement. ﴿Will you deny [the blessing of hearing from below] or [any] other?﴾ And there is nothing of what I have informed you of concerning the conditions of the Hereafter except that I have established for you in this world that by which you may be guided to knowledge of its occurrence.

When the Day of Resurrection comes, with its many aspects, its long and renowned standing-places of terror, and its great affairs and momentous matters in each of them, He mentioned some of what this time brings about in terms of recognizing the disobedient and the obedient, through signs that God made a means of knowing them. He said: ﴿So on that Day﴾, meaning: it follows from the Day when the sky splits open, because ﴿none will be asked﴾ a question of inquiry and seeking information, but a question of rebuke, reproach and censure. That is because it will not be said to him, "Did you do such-and-such?" Rather, it will be said to him, "Why did you do such-and-such?" This is in addition to the fact that that Day is long, and it has many aspects: at times one is questioned in it, and at times one is not questioned. The matter is at the utmost severity. Each of these aspects is called a day. It has already passed in al-Fatiha that "day" (yawm) is an expression for a time that extends until the end of a determined matter within it, whether marked by night, day, or something else, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To your Lord, on that Day, is the driving﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 30], meaning: a day when the soul reaches the collarbones. It does not belong only to night or only to day. He made the verb passive (﴿yus'alu﴾, "is asked") to magnify the matter, indicating that the condition of one who confesses his sin is not specific to one era rather than another. Rather, everyone who wishes to know it will know it. He placed the pronoun before mention, because it is more prominent in rank, in order to convey exclusivity. He made the pronoun singular for the sake of the wording, so He said: ﴿concerning his sin﴾, meaning: his sin alone. The virtuous, however, will be asked about his good deed as an honour to him and as a rebuke to those below him.

Since humankind is the greatest object of this, and for this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) was one of them, and since recognition through the familiar witness is greater in making things known, and since knowledge of the states of what is manifest is easier, He put them first and said: ﴿humankind﴾. And since knowledge of the states of the manifest does not necessarily entail knowledge of the states of the hidden, He made clear that all of it is easy for Him, glory be to Him, and so He said: ﴿nor jinn﴾.

Since this distinction is among the greatest of blessings, lest the confusion lead to alarming some of the obedient ones, by making them a means of harm or a cause of reproach through asking about them, He said: ﴿So which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?﴾ That is: the One who nurtured each of you with things about which there is no hope of denying and no concealment. ﴿Will you deny?﴾ Is it the blessing of the forelock's grasp, or the blessing of something other than it?

Since the discourse has been general, he made clear that it is specific to the recognition of the criminal from others, not to reproach for the sin or other states. So he said, giving the reason for not asking: ﴿They will be known﴾, that is, to everyone, ﴿the criminals﴾, that is, those who are deeply immersed in this attribute, ﴿by their marks﴾, that is, the signs in which God has shaped their sins, making them manifest after they were hidden, and clearly indicative of them, just as it is known that when night comes it is not hidden from anyone at all, and likewise day and the like, to anyone other than the blind. And those marks, God knows best, are blueness of the eyes, blackness of the faces, blindness, deafness, walking on their faces, and the like. Just as the good-doers are known by their marks: the whiteness and radiance of their faces, their smiling, and the blaze and the white markings (on hands and feet) and the like.
